solution.concept_anchor: Speaker holds office during pleasure of House
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students associate the Governor with all state-level executive powers and assume the Speaker, like the Governor's appointees, serves at the Governor's pleasure.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Speaker does not hold office at the pleasure of the Governor — that would make the Speaker subordinate to the executive, contradicting constitutional design.
Eliminate (c): The Speaker cannot be removed by the Chief Minister — no such provision exists in Articles 178–179.
Eliminate (d): 'Until the next general election' is imprecise — the Speaker continues even after dissolution until the new Assembly meets, not merely until elections.
Confirm (b): Article 179 establishes that the Speaker holds office during the pleasure of the Legislative Assembly — the House, not the Governor, is the authority.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students frequently conflate the Governor's supervisory role over state executive offices with the Speaker's tenure. Since the Governor appoints and can dismiss Ministers, many assume a similar relationship with the Speaker. In reality, the constitutional design deliberately insulates the Speaker from executive interference — the Speaker holds office during the pleasure of the House (not the Governor), making the legislature, not the executive, the final authority over the Speaker's continuance.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 178 provides for the election of the Speaker by members of the Legislative Assembly from amongst themselves. Article 179 governs the conditions under which the Speaker vacates office. The Speaker does not hold office at the pleasure of the Governor or the Chief Minister — this insulates the presiding officer from executive interference.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Governor has no authority over the Speaker's tenure. The Speaker is elected by and answerable to the House, not the executive.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Speaker holds office during the pleasure of the Legislative Assembly. Removal requires a resolution passed by an effective majority (majority of all then members).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Chief Minister has no constitutional power to remove the Speaker — that authority vests exclusively in the House.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 'Until the next general election' misstates the position — the Speaker continues even after dissolution, until the newly constituted Assembly first meets.

Value Addition:
• The Speaker's resignation is addressed to the Deputy Speaker, not the Governor.
• The Speaker vacates office when they cease to be a member of the Assembly.
• This design mirrors the Lok Sabha Speaker's position — both are elected by and answerable to their respective Houses.

solution.concept_anchor: Removal procedure Article 179(c) effective majority

statement_analysis.statement: A resolution for the removal of the Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly requires a majority of all the then members of the Assembly.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 179(c) prescribes an effective majority — a majority of all then members (not merely a majority of those present and voting), making this a higher threshold than a simple majority.

statement_analysis.statement: Before moving a resolution for the removal of the Speaker, a notice of at least 14 days must be given.
statement_analysis.reason: The constitutional requirement of 14-day advance notice is mandatory — it is not merely a convention but a procedural safeguard built into Article 179(c).

statement_analysis.statement: During the proceedings on a resolution for the Speaker's removal, the Speaker is prohibited from presiding over the House but retains the right to participate in debate.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker has the right to vote in the first instance during removal proceedings — unlike their normal role where they vote only on a tie. However, the Deputy Speaker presides during this resolution, so the statement's characterisation of the Speaker's role is partially misstated.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students who know Statements 1 and 2 are correct may assume Statement 3 is also correct given the general principle of speaker participation in removal motions.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Article 179(c) specifies 'majority of all the then members' — this is effective majority, not simple majority. Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: The 14-day notice requirement is explicitly stated in Article 179(c) — it is mandatory, not discretionary. Statement 2 is correct.

Verify Statement 3: The Speaker may vote in the first instance during removal proceedings — this is a unique right. But the statement says the Speaker is 'prohibited from presiding' which is correct, yet implies the Speaker cannot vote in the first instance, which is false. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Since Statements 1 and 2 are correct and Statement 3 is incorrect, the answer is (c) — 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the trap. Many students know that during removal proceedings, the Deputy Speaker presides — this part is true. But the statement then conflates 'not presiding' with 'cannot vote in first instance,' which is false. The Speaker uniquely retains the right to vote in the first instance (not merely a casting vote) during removal proceedings. Students who partially know this provision will either accept Statement 3 as correct (choosing option d) or reject it for the wrong reason.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 179(c) of the Constitution establishes the procedure for removing the Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly. This provision contains several specific requirements that are frequently tested.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The removal resolution requires a majority of all the then members of the Assembly — this is the 'effective majority' standard, higher than a simple majority of those present and voting.
• Statement 2 — Correct: A 14-day advance notice is constitutionally mandatory before moving such a resolution. This safeguard prevents sudden moves against the Speaker.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: While the Deputy Speaker presides during the removal proceedings (not the Speaker), the Speaker uniquely retains the right to vote in the first instance — unlike normal sessions where the Speaker votes only on a tie. The statement incorrectly implies the Speaker cannot exercise a first-instance vote.

Value Addition:
• The same effective majority (majority of all then members) applies for removal of the Deputy Speaker.
• The Governor is removed by the President (executive pleasure) — contrast with the Speaker's democratic removal procedure.
• The 14-day notice requirement is a constitutional provision under Article 179, not merely a convention.

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker continues post-dissolution until new Assembly meets

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly vacates office as soon as the Assembly is dissolved.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 179 explicitly provides that the Speaker does NOT vacate office merely on dissolution of the Assembly — they continue until the newly constituted Assembly first meets, ensuring institutional continuity.

statement_analysis.statement: A Minister in the state cabinet, unlike the Speaker, continues in office after the dissolution of the Assembly until a new government is sworn in.
statement_analysis.reason: Ministers vacate office on the dissolution of the Assembly (or technically hold office as a caretaker until a new government is formed); they do not enjoy the same constitutional continuity provision as the Speaker under Article 179.

statement_analysis.statement: If the Speaker of a Legislative Assembly submits their resignation, it must be addressed to the Deputy Speaker of the Assembly.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Article 179(b), the Speaker's resignation is addressed to the Deputy Speaker — this is the correct procedure and Statement 3 is therefore correct, not incorrect.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) appeals to students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong but mistakenly accept Statement 2 as a valid contrast, missing that Ministers' continuance is as 'caretaker' only, not a constitutional right comparable to the Speaker.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 179 states the Speaker continues even after dissolution until the new Assembly meets — so the claim that Speaker vacates 'as soon as Assembly is dissolved' is incorrect. Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Ministers constitutionally vacate office on dissolution; while convention allows caretaker continuation, it is not a constitutional right comparable to the Speaker's position. The claim that Ministers 'continue in office' is overstated — Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: The Speaker's resignation is indeed addressed to the Deputy Speaker per Article 179(b) — Statement 3 is correct, not incorrect.
The question asks which are NOT correct — Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct, making the answer (b) 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The dissolution trap is one of the most tested distinctions in this topic. Many students assume all holders of constitutional office vacate on dissolution. Statement 1 exploits this assumption. Statement 2 introduces a plausible-sounding contrast with Ministers that actually overstates the Minister's continuation — Ministers are caretakers by convention, not by a dedicated constitutional provision like Article 179. Students who confuse constitutional right with political convention will accept Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 179 of the Constitution contains a critical continuity provision for the Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly. Unlike most other constitutional offices, the Speaker is not displaced by the dissolution of the Assembly.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: The Speaker does not vacate on dissolution. Article 179 expressly provides that the Speaker continues in office until the newly constituted Assembly first meets. This ensures institutional continuity and an orderly transfer of powers.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct: Ministers vacate office on dissolution of the Assembly. While political convention permits them to continue as a caretaker government until successors are sworn in, this is not a constitutional right comparable to the Speaker's position under Article 179.
• Statement 3 — Correct (and therefore not the answer): The Speaker's resignation is addressed to the Deputy Speaker under Article 179(b). This is constitutionally accurate.

Value Addition:
• The Speaker vacates office when they cease to be a member of the Assembly (other than by dissolution).
• The continuity principle for the Speaker mirrors the provision for the Lok Sabha Speaker under Article 94.
• The Rajya Sabha Chairman (Vice President) has no equivalent dissolution-continuity issue since the Rajya Sabha is a permanent House.

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker adjournment vs Governor prorogation and casting vote

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly can adjourn the House sine die.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker has the power to adjourn the House — including sine die adjournment (adjournment without fixing a date of resumption). Prorogation, however, is the prerogative of the Governor.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker exercises a casting vote in the first instance on all procedural matters to expedite business.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker does NOT vote in the first instance on ordinary matters — the Speaker exercises only a casting vote, and only when there is a tie. The sole exception is during a removal resolution against the Speaker, where the Speaker may vote in the first instance.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker's certificate that a Bill is a Money Bill is final and cannot be challenged in any court of law.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 199 provides that the Speaker's decision on whether a Bill is a Money Bill is final, and no court can question it — making this one of the few non-reviewable exercises of constitutional authority.

statement_analysis.statement: The Governor prorogues the Assembly on the advice of the Speaker.
statement_analysis.reason: The Governor prorogues the Assembly on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Cabinet), not the Speaker. The Speaker's powers relate to adjournment; prorogation is an executive function.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only two' tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as correct but mistakenly also count Statement 4 as correct, believing the Governor acts on the Speaker's advice for prorogation.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Adjournment (including sine die) is the Speaker's power; prorogation belongs to the Governor. Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: The Speaker votes only on a tie (casting vote) — not 'in the first instance on all procedural matters.' Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 199 makes the Speaker's Money Bill certificate non-justiciable. Statement 3 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: The Governor prorogues on Cabinet advice, not the Speaker's advice. Statement 4 is incorrect.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct — the answer is (a) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the 'casting vote' confusion. During removal proceedings, the Speaker can vote in the first instance — students who know this exception may overgeneralise it to ordinary sessions. Statement 4 exploits the natural assumption that the Speaker, as head of the House, would advise on prorogation — in reality, prorogation is an executive act done on Cabinet advice.
solution.final_explanation:
The Speaker's powers over House business are extensive but have specific constitutional boundaries. Four common claims are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Speaker has the power to adjourn the House, including sine die adjournment. Prorogation (ending a session) is different — it is the Governor's prerogative exercised on Cabinet advice.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: In ordinary proceedings, the Speaker casts a vote only when there is a tie (casting vote, not first-instance vote). The first-instance voting right exists only during a removal resolution against the Speaker.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 199 provides that the Speaker's certification of a Money Bill is final and non-justiciable — courts cannot question it.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The Governor prorogues the Assembly on the advice of the Council of Ministers, not the Speaker. The Speaker's domain is adjournment, not prorogation.

Only two statements (1 and 3) are correct.

Value Addition:
• Adjournment ends a sitting; prorogation ends a session; dissolution ends the Assembly itself.
• The Speaker can also call an emergency sitting of the House in some states under rules of procedure.
• The non-justiciability of the Money Bill certificate has been a subject of political controversy at both Centre and state levels.

Kihoto Hollohan Case (1992) and Its Implications for Speaker's Powers

solution.concept_anchor: Kihoto Hollohan Tenth Schedule judicial review limitation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know Kihoto Hollohan upheld the Tenth Schedule may assume paragraph 7 (judicial review bar) was also upheld, making A-3 plausible — but paragraph 7 was struck down.
elimination_logic: Match A (Kihoto Hollohan case): The case established that the Speaker's order under the Tenth Schedule is subject to judicial review only after a final order — not during proceedings. A matches with 2.
Match B (Paragraph 7 of Tenth Schedule): Paragraph 7 originally barred judicial review of Speaker's decisions — the Supreme Court struck it down as unconstitutional. B matches with 4.

Match C (Merger exception): The merger exception requires at least two-thirds of members of a legislature party to merge with another party — the Speaker decides whether this threshold is met. C matches with 1.
Match D (Nabam Rebia case): The SC held that a Speaker facing a pending removal notice cannot adjudicate disqualification petitions — conflict of interest principle. D matches with 3.
The correct combination is A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is in B and D. Students who partially know Kihoto Hollohan may pair paragraph 7 with 'judicial review is final after Speaker's order' (merging the holding with the provision struck down). Similarly, Nabam Rebia is a less-known case — students may confuse its holding (Speaker cannot decide disqualification when facing removal notice) with the Kihoto principle. The conflation of these two cases' holdings is the primary distractor mechanism.
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) has generated significant constitutional jurisprudence. This question tests precision on four distinct legal concepts.

• A-2: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) established that the Speaker's orders under the Tenth Schedule are subject to judicial review — but only after a final order is passed, not at an interim stage. Courts cannot intervene during proceedings.
• B-4: Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule originally barred all judicial review of the Speaker's decisions. The Supreme Court struck down paragraph 7 as unconstitutional in Kihoto Hollohan — the bar on judicial review was removed.
• C-1: The merger exception under the Tenth Schedule permits a political party merger without disqualification, provided at least two-thirds of the legislative party members participate. The Speaker determines whether a valid merger has occurred.
• D-3: In Nabam Rebia (2016), the Supreme Court held that when a notice of motion for the Speaker's removal is pending, the Speaker loses jurisdiction to decide disqualification petitions — the conflict of interest disables the authority.

Correct combination: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 → Option (b).

Value Addition:
• The Nabam Rebia case has been referred to a larger Constitution Bench — the law on this point is still evolving.
• The Tenth Schedule was added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985.
• The Speaker acts as a 'tribunal' under the Tenth Schedule — this is why the decision has the force of law.

solution.concept_anchor: Money Bill Speaker certificate finality Article 199
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) appeals to students who verify both A and R as factually true without rigorously testing whether the non-justiciability of the certificate is caused by the Legislative Council's lack of amendment power, or by an independent constitutional provision.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? A states that in a bicameral state legislature, the Legislative Council cannot reject or amend a Money Bill certified by the Speaker. This is correct — the Council can only make recommendations which the Assembly may accept or reject.
Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? R states that the Speaker's certificate under Article 199 is final and no court can question it. This is also correct — Article 199 explicitly provides this finality.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? The Council's inability to reject/amend a Money Bill (A) flows from the constitutional provisions for Money Bills (parallel to Article 110 at Centre) — not from the Speaker's certificate being non-justiciable. The certificate's finality (R) relates to judicial non-review; the Council's limited role (A) is a separate constitutional design feature. R does not cause A.
A is correct, R is correct, but R does NOT explain A — the answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both A and R are factually accurate, making option (a) the instinctive answer. The trap lies in the causal relationship. A student who quickly verifies both facts as true will choose (a). The rigorous analysis reveals that the Council's inability to reject a Money Bill is a constitutional design feature for bicameral balance — it is NOT caused by the Speaker's certificate being non-justiciable. These are two independent constitutional features of the Money Bill regime. Option (b) correctly identifies that both facts are true but causally unconnected.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 199 governs Money Bills in state legislatures with Legislative Councils. Two distinct constitutional features are tested here.

Assertion (A) — Correct: In a bicameral state legislature, the Legislative Council cannot reject or amend a Money Bill. It can only make recommendations, which the Assembly may accept or reject. This ensures financial legislation is not blocked by an unelected or indirectly elected upper house.

Reason (R) — Correct: Under Article 199, the Speaker's certificate that a Bill is a Money Bill is final and is not subject to judicial review. This finality clause is explicitly stated in the Constitution.

Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The Council's limited role in Money Bills is a constitutional design choice about the balance of power between two houses — it exists independent of the Speaker's certificate. The finality of the certificate relates to courts not being able to question it; it does not explain why the Council cannot amend or reject the Bill. These are two separate constitutional features operating in different spheres.

Correct answer: (b) — Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• Only 6 states have bicameral legislatures: UP, Maharashtra, Bihar, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.
• Unlike Parliament (Article 108), there is no provision for a joint sitting of State Assembly and Council.
• The Aadhaar Act's certification as a Money Bill at the Centre has parallels with state-level Money Bill controversies.

solution.concept_anchor: Nabam Rebia Arunachal Pradesh constitutional crisis sequence
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) tempts students who remember the Arunachal Pradesh crisis of 2016 but confuse the sequence of the Speaker's disqualification actions and the Supreme Court's intervention.
elimination_logic: Place Event 1 (52nd Amendment — Tenth Schedule): The Tenth Schedule was added in 1985 by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment — this is the earliest event.
Place Event 2 (Kihoto Hollohan judgment): The Supreme Court's landmark ruling on the Tenth Schedule came in 1992 — after the Amendment but before the Arunachal Pradesh crisis.
Place Event 3 (Arunachal Pradesh political crisis — Nabam Rebia case): The crisis and the SC's judgment in Nabam Rebia occurred in 2016 — after Kihoto Hollohan.

Place Event 4 (Subhash Desai case — SC direction on time limits): This Maharashtra-related case directing time-bound decisions on disqualification petitions is more recent — 2023. The correct order is 1 → 2 → 3 → 4, which is option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is temporal — students may confuse the 52nd Amendment (1985) with the 91st Amendment (2003, which increased the anti-defection provisions) and place events out of sequence. Additionally, the Subhash Desai case (2023) is recent enough that students may not be aware of it, leading them to conflate it with or place it before Nabam Rebia (2016).
solution.final_explanation:
The anti-defection jurisprudence evolved through distinct legislative and judicial milestones. Correct chronological placement requires knowing the precise years.

• 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1985): Added the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution — the foundational legislative event.
• Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992): The Supreme Court upheld the Tenth Schedule but struck down paragraph 7 (which barred judicial review) and established that courts can review Speaker's final orders.
• Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016): SC held that a Speaker facing a pending removal notice cannot adjudicate disqualification petitions — arose from the Arunachal Pradesh constitutional crisis.
• Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary (2023): SC directed that Speakers must decide disqualification petitions within a reasonable timeframe — further constraining Speaker's discretion on delay.

Correct sequence: 52nd Amendment (1985) → Kihoto Hollohan (1992) → Nabam Rebia (2016) → Subhash Desai (2023) → Option (d).

Value Addition:
• The 91st Amendment Act (2003) amended the Tenth Schedule to remove the provision allowing splits (one-third split) as a defence against disqualification.
• The Tenth Schedule applies to both Parliament and State Legislatures.
• Nabam Rebia has been referred to a larger Constitution Bench — the final position is still pending.

solution.concept_anchor: Nabam Rebia Speaker jurisdiction pending removal notice
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students know the Speaker is the sole adjudicating authority under the Tenth Schedule and may assume this authority is absolute, unaware of the Nabam Rebia limitation.
elimination_logic: Identify the key facts in the scenario: (1) The Speaker has received disqualification petitions against ruling party MLAs. (2) A notice of motion for the Speaker's removal has been given by opposition members.

Apply Nabam Rebia (2016): The Supreme Court held that when a notice of removal against the Speaker is pending, the Speaker loses jurisdiction to adjudicate disqualification petitions — conflict of interest principle applies.
Eliminate (a): The Speaker cannot proceed to decide the petitions in this situation — Nabam Rebia specifically bars this.
Eliminate (b): The High Court cannot directly decide Tenth Schedule petitions — it reviews Speaker's final orders, it does not substitute as primary adjudicator.
Eliminate (d): The Governor has no authority under the Tenth Schedule — disqualification is not an executive function.
Confirm (c): The Speaker's jurisdiction is suspended due to the pending removal notice — the correct principle from Nabam Rebia applies.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) exploits the very accurate fact that the Speaker is the sole adjudicating authority under the Tenth Schedule. Students who know this well-established principle will choose (a) without factoring in the Nabam Rebia exception. The Nabam Rebia ruling is a relatively recent and nuanced judicial limitation — it applies specifically when the Speaker's own removal is simultaneously at issue, creating a conflict of interest that disables the authority. Partially prepared students who know the general rule but not the exception will fall into this trap.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the application of the Nabam Rebia (2016) principle, which carves out a significant limitation on the Speaker's Tenth Schedule powers.

The applicable principle: When a notice of motion for the removal of the Speaker is pending before the House, the Speaker cannot exercise jurisdiction to decide disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule. The constitutional logic is the conflict of interest — the Speaker cannot act as adjudicator over the very MLAs whose defection might determine whether the Speaker retains the post.

Mapping to the scenario: The opposition has given a removal notice against the Speaker. Simultaneously, the Speaker holds disqualification petitions against ruling party MLAs. Nabam Rebia directly applies — the Speaker's authority is suspended for the duration that the removal notice remains pending.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: While the Speaker is ordinarily the sole authority under the Tenth Schedule, the pending removal notice suspends this jurisdiction per Nabam Rebia.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The High Court reviews final Speaker orders — it does not act as the primary adjudicating authority under the Tenth Schedule.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Speaker's jurisdiction is displaced by the pending removal notice — the Nabam Rebia ruling governs.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Governor has no role in Tenth Schedule proceedings — disqualification is not an executive function.

Value Addition:
• Nabam Rebia has been referred to a larger Constitution Bench — the final position on this limitation is still under judicial consideration.
• The Deputy Speaker presides when the Speaker's removal resolution is being considered.
• Tenth Schedule proceedings are quasi-judicial in nature — the Speaker acts as a tribunal.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) Telangana is a strong distractor because it is a newly formed state (2014) and students may not know it inherited or established a Legislative Council, making them doubt its bicameral status.
elimination_logic: Verify Uttar Pradesh: UP has a Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) — confirmed bicameral.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The UPSC frequently tests the list of bicameral states. Odisha is a persistent distractor because it is a large state and students sometimes confuse it with Bihar or Karnataka. Telangana is the other common source of confusion — being a new state (2014), students may not be certain it has a Council. The correct six bicameral states are UP, Maharashtra, Bihar, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana — Odisha is not among them.
solution.final_explanation:
As of the current constitutional position, only six Indian states have bicameral legislatures (with both a Legislative Assembly and a Legislative Council): Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.

• Option (a) Uttar Pradesh — Has a Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad). It is one of the oldest and largest bicameral state legislatures.
• Option (b) Telangana — Has a Legislative Council, inherited from the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014. Confirmed bicameral.
• Option (c) Odisha — Does NOT have a Legislative Council. It is a unicameral state. This is the odd one out.
• Option (d) Karnataka — Has a Legislative Council. Karnataka is one of the six confirmed bicameral states.

Value Addition:
• Jammu & Kashmir had a bicameral legislature before losing statehood in 2019 — it is now a Union Territory with a unicameral legislature.
• The Constitution (under Article 169) permits creation or abolition of Legislative Councils by Parliament on the basis of a resolution passed by the concerned state's Assembly.
• West Bengal and Rajasthan have passed resolutions to create Legislative Councils but they are not yet operational.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 212 legislative immunity Raja Ram Pal exception

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 212, courts are completely barred from inquiring into the proceedings of a State Legislature, and no exception to this immunity has been recognised.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 212 bars courts from inquiring into legislative proceedings, but the Supreme Court in Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker (2007) recognised that courts can intervene when there is an allegation of unconstitutional action — the immunity is not absolute.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly is the custodian of the privileges of the House and decides whether a breach of privilege has occurred before referring it to the Privileges Committee.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker is constitutionally recognised as the custodian of the House's privileges under Article 194 and plays the primary role in determining whether a prima facie case of breach of privilege exists before the matter is referred to the Privileges Committee.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) appeals to students who know both Article 212 and the Speaker's custodial role, not realising that Statement 1 overstates the immunity by adding 'no exception has been recognised.'
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 212 does provide immunity from court inquiry into legislative proceedings. However, Raja Ram Pal (2007) established that unconstitutional actions are not shielded — the immunity is not absolute. Adding 'no exception has been recognised' makes Statement 1 incorrect.

Evaluate Statement 2: The Speaker's role as custodian of House privileges under Article 194, including preliminary determination of breach of privilege before referral to the Privileges Committee, is accurate. Statement 2 is correct.
Since Statement 1 is incorrect and Statement 2 is correct, the answer is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses the word 'completely' and the phrase 'no exception has been recognised' — both scope-extension qualifiers that convert a largely true statement into a false one. Students who recall Article 212's immunity provision will affirm Statement 1 without recalling the Raja Ram Pal exception. This is a classic UPSC technique of embedding an absolute qualifier to invalidate an otherwise plausible statement.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 194 and 212 together define the privilege framework for state legislatures.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 212 does insulate legislative proceedings from court inquiry, but this immunity is not absolute. The Supreme Court in Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker (2007) held that courts can intervene when there is an allegation of unconstitutional action — such as expulsion of a member in violation of the Constitution. The phrase 'no exception has been recognised' makes Statement 1 factually incorrect.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Speaker under Article 194 is the custodian of the House's collective and individual privileges. The Speaker makes a preliminary determination of whether a prima facie breach of privilege has occurred, after which the matter is referred to the Privileges Committee for detailed examination.

Value Addition:
• Article 194 for state legislatures corresponds to Article 105 for Parliament — both govern privileges.
• Privileges include freedom of speech in the House, immunity from court proceedings for things said or done in the House, and the right to regulate internal proceedings.
• The question of codifying parliamentary privileges has been debated — currently, they are partly constitutional and partly based on the British Parliament's precedents.

solution.concept_anchor: Panel of chairpersons presides when both Speaker Deputy Speaker absent
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students logically assume the Governor, as the constitutional head of the state, would step in when the Assembly's presiding officers are both absent.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a) Pro-tem Speaker: A Pro-tem Speaker is appointed temporarily before the election of the regular Speaker — not a standing mechanism for filling in during absence.

Eliminate (c) Governor: The Governor is the executive head; the Governor does not preside over the Legislative Assembly's proceedings — that would violate the separation of legislative and executive functions.
Eliminate (d) Chief Minister: The Chief Minister has no constitutional role in presiding over the Assembly.

Confirm (b): When both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are absent, a member from the panel of chairpersons (nominated by the Speaker) presides — this is the constitutionally prescribed mechanism under Article 180.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Governor trap is the most common error here. Students who know that the Governor is the constitutional head of the state and that many appointments flow through the Governor assume the Governor would preside in the absence of both presiding officers. In reality, Article 180 creates a panel of chairpersons — members nominated by the Speaker — to handle exactly this situation. The Governor has no role in the internal proceedings of the Assembly.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 180 governs the situation where both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly are absent from a sitting.

• Option (a) Pro-tem Speaker — Incorrect: A Pro-tem Speaker is a temporary arrangement made specifically before the election of a Speaker in a newly constituted Assembly — it is not the standing mechanism for filling absences of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
• Option (b) A member from the panel of chairpersons — Correct: Under Article 180, when both are absent, a member from the panel of chairpersons (persons nominated in advance by the Speaker) presides over the House. This is the constitutionally prescribed mechanism.
• Option (c) Governor — Incorrect: The Governor is the executive head and has no role in presiding over the proceedings of the Legislative Assembly. Legislative and executive functions are separated.
• Option (d) Chief Minister — Incorrect: The Chief Minister has no constitutional authority to preside over the Assembly.

Value Addition:
• The panel of chairpersons is nominated by the Speaker — not elected by the House.
• When a resolution for the Speaker's removal is being considered, the Deputy Speaker presides — even if the Speaker is present (the Speaker steps down).
• The same panel mechanism exists at the Centre under Article 95 for the Lok Sabha.

solution.concept_anchor: Chairman Legislative Council Money Bill certification exclusive to Speaker
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students know the removal procedure for both the Speaker and Chairman involves a 14-day notice, but may incorrectly assume the majority required differs — in fact both require effective majority.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly certifies Money Bills under Article 199 — the Chairman of the Legislative Council has NO such power. This pairing — 'Speaker: Money Bill certification' — is correctly matched.

Evaluate (b): The Vice-Chairman (not the Speaker) presides when a resolution for the Chairman's removal is considered. If option (b) says the Chairman presides during removal proceedings, it is incorrectly matched.
Evaluate (c): Both the Speaker and the Chairman are removed by a majority of all then members with 14-day notice — if the option alters this, it is wrong.

Evaluate (d): The Chairman of the Council does not certify Money Bills — that is exclusively the Speaker's power. If (d) attributes Money Bill certification to the Chairman, it is incorrectly matched.
Option (a) is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The key trap is attributing Money Bill certification to the Chairman of the Legislative Council — which is incorrect. Only the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly has this power. Students who study the Speaker's powers may apply them to the Chairman by analogy, not realising the Constitution specifically restricts Money Bill certification to the Speaker of the Assembly.
solution.final_explanation:
The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly and the Chairman of the Legislative Council are both presiding officers elected by their respective Houses, but their powers differ in important ways.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Money Bill certification under Article 199 is exclusively the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly's power. The Chairman of the Council has no role in Money Bill certification — this is a critical distinction.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: When a resolution for the Chairman's removal is being considered, the Vice-Chairman (not the Chairman) presides — parallel to the Speaker/Deputy Speaker arrangement.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: The removal procedure for both the Speaker and Chairman requires a majority of all then members (effective majority) with 14-day notice — any option that assigns different majorities to them is wrong.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: The Chairman of the Legislative Council does not certify Money Bills. Attributing this power to the Chairman is a factual error.

Value Addition:
• Both the Speaker and the Chairman are elected by members of their respective Houses — same election procedure.
• The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is the Vice President of India — not elected by Rajya Sabha members. This is the key distinction between the Chairman of the Council of States and state Legislative Councils.
• There is no provision for a joint sitting of a State Assembly and its Legislative Council — unlike Article 108 for Parliament.

solution.concept_anchor: Articles 178 179 180 Speaker constitutional provisions

statement_analysis.statement: Article 178 provides for the election of both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly from among the members of the Assembly.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 178 specifically provides that the Legislative Assembly shall choose two members of the Assembly to be the Speaker and Deputy Speaker respectively — both are elected by members of the Assembly from amongst themselves.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 180 empowers the Deputy Speaker or, in the Deputy Speaker's absence, a member of the panel of chairpersons to perform the duties of the Speaker's office during a vacancy.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 180 provides that when the Speaker's office is vacant, or the Speaker is absent, the Deputy Speaker shall perform the duties; if the Deputy Speaker is also absent or the Deputy Speaker's office is also vacant, such member of the Assembly as the President may appoint (per convention, from a panel) shall perform those duties.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 179 provides that the Speaker must vacate office upon dissolution of the Assembly so as to enable the newly elected Assembly to choose its own presiding officer.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 179 explicitly provides that the Speaker does NOT vacate office on dissolution of the Assembly — the Speaker continues in office until the newly constituted Assembly first meets. This is a deliberate continuity provision, not a requirement to vacate.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) tempts students who accept all three statements as correct because they reflect logically consistent institutional arrangements — the error in Statement 3 requires precise knowledge of Article 179's text.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Article 178 explicitly covers both Speaker and Deputy Speaker elections — both elected from among Assembly members. Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: Article 180 creates the hierarchical substitute mechanism — Deputy Speaker first, then panel member. Statement 2 is correct.

Verify Statement 3: Article 179 says the Speaker does NOT vacate on dissolution — the Speaker continues until the new Assembly meets. Statement 3 is incorrect — it directly contradicts the text of Article 179.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Statement 3 is incorrect — the answer is (b) 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the intuitive assumption that when an Assembly is dissolved and a new one elected, the old Speaker should vacate to allow fresh selection. This seems logically correct to students who reason from first principles rather than constitutional text. Article 179's continuity provision — designed to prevent an institutional vacuum — is counterintuitive and is therefore a high-frequency UPSC trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 178–180 contain the foundational provisions for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 178 provides for the election of both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker from among the members of the Assembly. The House chooses two of its members for these offices respectively.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 180 creates a hierarchical mechanism for filling the Speaker's role during vacancy or absence — Deputy Speaker first, then a member from the panel of chairpersons.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: This directly contradicts Article 179, which expressly provides that the Speaker does NOT vacate office on dissolution. The Speaker continues until the newly constituted Assembly first meets — a deliberate institutional continuity measure.

Value Addition:
• The Speaker's resignation is addressed to the Deputy Speaker; the Deputy Speaker's resignation is addressed to the Speaker.
• The Speaker vacates office only upon ceasing to be a member of the Assembly (other than by dissolution), resignation, or removal by a resolution of the House.
• Article 179's continuity provision prevents a constitutional vacuum during the interregnum between dissolution and the new Assembly's first sitting.

solution.concept_anchor: Merger exception two-thirds threshold Tenth Schedule Speaker decides
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because 'one-half' sounds like a supermajority that appropriately balances the simple majority and two-thirds thresholds, and students may confuse this with other constitutional thresholds.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a) one-third: This was the original provision under the Tenth Schedule for 'splits' — but the 91st Amendment (2003) removed the split defence. One-third is no longer the applicable threshold.
Eliminate (b) one-half: No constitutional provision under the Tenth Schedule uses a one-half threshold for the merger exception — this is a fabricated option.
Eliminate (d) three-fourths: Three-fourths is used in other constitutional contexts (e.g., ratification of amendments under Article 368) but not for the Tenth Schedule merger exception.
Confirm (c) two-thirds: The Tenth Schedule's merger exception requires at least two-thirds of the members of the legislature party to merge with another political party.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) one-third exploits students' memory of the original Tenth Schedule provision that allowed a one-third split to avoid disqualification. The 91st Amendment (2003) removed this split exception, but many students retain the one-third figure. Option (b) one-half sounds like a reasonable supermajority. Students who know 'two-thirds' is used in constitutional contexts may hesitate between options (b) and (c) — only precise knowledge of the Tenth Schedule's exact text resolves this.
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) contains an exception for political party mergers. A merger is recognised as valid — and members who participate are not disqualified for defection — only when the threshold specified in the Schedule is met.

• Option (a) one-third — Incorrect: One-third was the threshold for the 'split' exception in the original Tenth Schedule. The 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) removed the split defence entirely. One-third no longer has any relevance under the Tenth Schedule.
• Option (b) one-half — Incorrect: No constitutional provision under the Tenth Schedule uses a one-half threshold. This is a plausible-sounding but fabricated threshold.
• Option (c) two-thirds — Correct: The merger exception under the Tenth Schedule requires at least two-thirds of the members of the legislature party to merge with another political party. The Speaker decides whether this threshold has been met.
• Option (d) three-fourths — Incorrect: Three-fourths is a threshold used in other constitutional contexts, such as the ratification of certain constitutional amendments, but not in the Tenth Schedule's merger exception.

Value Addition:
• The Speaker determines whether a valid merger has occurred — this decision is subject to judicial review after a final order (Kihoto Hollohan).
• The 91st Amendment also added a provision capping the size of the Council of Ministers at 15% of the Assembly's strength.
• A 'merger' under the Tenth Schedule requires the original political party to also merge — not just the legislature party members.

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker's disciplinary powers naming suspension expunging

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker can 'name' a member as a formal disciplinary action that precedes suspension from the House.
statement_analysis.reason: Naming a member is a formal step in the disciplinary process — the Speaker names the disorderly member, which is a precondition to suspension. The named member can then be suspended by the House on a motion.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker can unilaterally suspend a member from the House for the remainder of the session without any motion being moved by the House.
statement_analysis.reason: While the Speaker can direct a member to withdraw from the House for a day (immediate power), suspension for longer periods typically requires a motion to be moved in the House and passed. The Speaker does not unilaterally suspend without a House motion for extended periods — the House itself suspends via a motion.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker can expunge remarks made by a member from the official record of proceedings, and expunged remarks do not form part of the published debates.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker has the power to expunge objectionable, indecorous, or unparliamentary remarks from the official record. Once expunged, those remarks do not appear in the published proceedings of the House.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) appeals to students who, knowing the Speaker's general disciplinary authority, assume all three statements are correct without distinguishing the Speaker's direct powers from those requiring a House motion.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Naming is a standard parliamentary disciplinary step preceding suspension — it is a recognised and formally established procedure. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: While the Speaker has the power to direct a member to withdraw for the day, a full session-long suspension requires the House to pass a motion. The Speaker cannot unilaterally impose extended suspension. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: The Speaker's power to expunge remarks from official records is well established — expunged remarks do not appear in published debates. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — the answer is (a) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the trap. The Speaker's power to maintain order is extensive but not unlimited. Students who know the Speaker can suspend members conflate the Speaker's immediate powers (directing a member to withdraw for the day) with longer-term suspension (which requires a House motion). The partial truth in Statement 2 — that the Speaker does have suspension-related powers — makes the full statement seem correct to students who do not parse the distinction carefully.
solution.final_explanation:
The Speaker's powers to maintain order in the Legislative Assembly span multiple mechanisms, each with different procedural requirements.

• Statement 1 — Correct: 'Naming' a member is a formal disciplinary measure. The Speaker names the member exhibiting disorderly conduct — this is a precondition to suspension and signals a serious escalation of the disciplinary process.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: While the Speaker can order a member to withdraw for the remainder of the day (an immediate power), extended suspension for the remainder of a session requires the House to pass a motion to that effect. The Speaker does not have unilateral authority for session-long suspension — it requires the House's concurrence.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Speaker has the power to expunge objectionable remarks from the official record. Members cannot compel their expunged remarks to remain — once the Speaker orders expunction, those remarks do not appear in published debates.

Value Addition:
• Contempt of the House is different from breach of privilege — the Speaker refers contempt matters to the Privileges Committee.
• The distinction between the Speaker's immediate powers and the House's suspension powers reflects the separation between the presiding officer's authority and the collective authority of the House.
• Courts generally cannot inquire into whether a member was validly suspended — Article 212 protects internal proceedings.

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker committee powers ex-officio chairperson rules committee

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker nominates members to all legislative committees but does not personally chair any of them, as presiding over the House and chairing committees simultaneously would create a conflict of roles.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker is the ex-officio head of both the Rules Committee and the General Purposes Committee — the Speaker does personally chair specific committees, not merely nominate members. The premise that the Speaker cannot chair committees is constitutionally incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker can refer a Bill to a Select Committee or Joint Committee and has the authority to decide the composition of such committees and their terms of reference.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker has the power to refer Bills to Select or Joint Committees and determines both the composition of these committees and their specific terms of reference — this is part of the Speaker's central role in the legislative process.

statement_analysis.statement: The Public Accounts Committee of the State Legislature is chaired by the Speaker ex officio, making it the primary committee under the Speaker's direct control.
statement_analysis.reason: The Public Accounts Committee is not chaired by the Speaker ex officio — its chairperson is typically a member nominated by the Speaker, often from the opposition. The Speaker is ex-officio head of the Rules Committee and General Purposes Committee, not the Public Accounts Committee.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) appeals to students who are unsure about which specific committees the Speaker chairs and assume all three statements are incorrect, not realising Statement 2 is accurate.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The Speaker is ex-officio head of the Rules Committee and General Purposes Committee — the Speaker does chair committees. Statement 1's claim that the Speaker 'does not personally chair any' is incorrect.

Evaluate Statement 2: The Speaker's power to refer Bills to Select/Joint Committees and determine their composition and terms of reference is accurate. Statement 2 is correct — it should NOT be selected as incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: The Public Accounts Committee is chaired by a nominated member (typically from the opposition) — the Speaker is not ex-officio head. Statement 3 is incorrect.
The question asks which are NOT correct — Statements 1 and 3 are not correct — the answer is (b) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 deploys the ex-officio trap — students know the Speaker is ex-officio head of some committees and may assume the Public Accounts Committee (being the most prominent legislative oversight committee) is among them. In reality, the PAC is chaired by an opposition member (by convention), not the Speaker. Statement 1 uses a plausible institutional logic argument — but the Speaker does chair the Rules and General Purposes Committees as ex-officio head.
solution.final_explanation:
The Speaker's role in the committee system is extensive but has specific boundaries that are frequently misunderstood.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: The Speaker is the ex-officio head of the Rules Committee and the General Purposes Committee. The claim that the Speaker does not personally chair any committee is factually wrong.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Speaker has full authority to refer Bills to Select or Joint Committees and to determine both the composition and terms of reference of such committees. This is a key legislative scrutiny power.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: The Public Accounts Committee is not chaired by the Speaker ex officio. By convention (mirroring the Lok Sabha practice), the PAC is chaired by a member of the opposition, ensuring accountability. The Speaker nominates the chairperson but does not chair it personally.

Value Addition:
• The Business Advisory Committee, which allocates time for legislative business, operates under the Speaker's direction — the Speaker typically chairs it.
• The committee system is considered crucial for detailed legislative scrutiny — state legislatures often under-utilise committees compared to Parliament.
• The Public Accounts Committee examines the Comptroller and Auditor General's report on state government expenditure.

solution.concept_anchor: Assembly Secretariat charged expenditure Consolidated Fund separation of powers
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? A states that the budget of the Legislative Assembly Secretariat is typically treated as charged expenditure on the Consolidated Fund of the State — not subject to vote by the legislature. This is correct — it parallels the Parliament Secretariat's financial arrangements.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? R states that recruitment and service conditions of Assembly Secretariat staff are governed by rules made by the Governor (not the Speaker). This is incorrect — the Speaker, not the Governor, controls the Assembly Secretariat and makes rules governing staff recruitment and service conditions.
Step 3 — Since A is correct but R is incorrect, the answer is (c).

Confirm: The final step names option (c) — this matches correct_option (c). Wait — re-checking: correct_option is set to 'd'. Re-verify: R claims Governor controls Secretariat staff — actually the Speaker controls this. R is incorrect. A is correct. So the answer should be (c). Correcting correct_option to 'c'.
solution.final_explanation:
The administrative and financial independence of the Legislative Assembly Secretariat is a key element of the separation of powers at the state level.

Assertion (A) — Correct: The budget of the Legislative Assembly Secretariat is treated as charged expenditure on the Consolidated Fund of the State. Charged expenditure is not subject to a vote by the legislature — it is automatically drawn from the Consolidated Fund. This ensures the legislature's administration is not subject to the executive's control over budget allocations.

Reason (R) — Incorrect: The service conditions and recruitment of Assembly Secretariat staff are governed by rules made by the Speaker — not the Governor. The Speaker controls the Secretariat independently of the state government. The Governor has no direct role in managing the Assembly Secretariat's staff. This independence is precisely what insulates the legislature from executive control.

Since A is correct and R is incorrect, the answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• The financial independence of the Secretariat (charged expenditure) reinforces the legislature's independence from the executive — a core separation-of-powers principle.
• The same principle applies to the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha Secretariats at the Centre.
• The Speaker's control over Secretariat staff prevents the executive from influencing the legislature's administrative machinery.

solution.concept_anchor: UK Speaker severs party ties India Speaker remains party member

statement_analysis.statement: In the United Kingdom, when a member of the House of Commons is elected as Speaker, they sever all ties with their political party and contest subsequent elections as an independent candidate — a convention that India has not adopted.
statement_analysis.reason: The UK parliamentary convention requires the Speaker to resign from their party upon election and subsequently stand for re-election as an independent — their constituency is uncontested by major parties. This convention exists in the UK but has not been adopted in India, where the Speaker typically remains a party member.

statement_analysis.statement: The Law Commission of India, through its reports, has recommended abolishing the position of Speaker and transferring the presiding officer's functions to a retired judge of the High Court, in order to ensure impartiality.
statement_analysis.reason: No Law Commission report has recommended abolishing the Speaker's position or transferring functions to a retired judge. Reform suggestions have focused on making the Speaker's office more independent (e.g., UK-style convention, fixed tenure) — not abolition of the office.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) appeals to students who verify Statement 1 as correct and then, uncertain about Statement 2, assume it might also be correct given the prevalence of judicial reform recommendations in India.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The UK convention of the Speaker severing party ties and contesting as an independent is well-documented. India has not adopted this convention — Indian Speakers remain party members. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: This claim about abolishing the Speaker's position is not supported by any Law Commission report. Reform suggestions involve making the existing office independent, not abolishing it. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 is correct, Statement 2 is incorrect — the answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the trap — it contains a plausible institutional argument (judicial impartiality for a presiding officer) that sounds like a reform suggestion someone might make, and students familiar with Law Commission reports may not be certain this specific recommendation was not made. The recommendation's authoritative attribution to the Law Commission makes it sound credible. In reality, reform suggestions have focused on UK-style party severance conventions and fixed tenures, not abolishing the Speaker's office.
solution.final_explanation:
The impartiality of the Speaker is a contested area where constitutional expectation diverges from Indian political practice.

• Statement 1 — Correct: In the UK, an elected Speaker resigns from their party, contests subsequent elections as an independent, and is not opposed by major parties in their constituency — the Speaker transcends partisan politics entirely. India has not adopted this convention. Indian Speakers typically remain members of the party that nominated them and may return to active party politics after leaving office.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No Law Commission report has recommended abolishing the Speaker's position or replacing it with a retired High Court judge. Reform suggestions in India — from scholars, parliamentary committees, and the N.C. Saxena Committee — have focused on adopting the UK-style convention of party severance and ensuring time-bound decisions on disqualification petitions.

Value Addition:
• The N.C. Saxena Committee recommended reforms including adopting UK-style conventions for the Speaker's impartiality.
• G.V. Mavalankar, the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha, is regarded as having set high standards of impartiality in the Indian context.
• The constitutional expectation of impartiality is reflected in the Speaker's power to certify Money Bills and adjudicate disqualification — both of which require neutral judgment.

Distinction Between Speaker of Legislative Assembly and Chairman of Legislative Council

solution.concept_anchor: No joint sitting state legislature bicameral deadlock resolution

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike Parliament (which has Article 108 for joint sittings), there is no constitutional provision for a joint sitting of the State Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council to resolve a deadlock between them.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution does not provide for a joint sitting of the two Houses of a bicameral state legislature. Unlike Article 108 at the Centre, no parallel provision exists for states — deadlocks between the Assembly and Council cannot be resolved through a joint sitting.

statement_analysis.statement: In a bicameral state legislature, if the Legislative Council rejects a Bill passed by the Assembly (other than a Money Bill), the Assembly can pass the Bill again in the next session and the Council's rejection will have no further effect.
statement_analysis.reason: There is no such provision in the Constitution for state legislatures — this conflates the state position with a misreading of Parliamentary procedure. For state legislatures, since there is no joint sitting, the Council's delaying power is the only check, and the Assembly cannot automatically override the Council by mere re-passage.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chairman of the Legislative Council presides over its proceedings but has no role in the Money Bill process — the Money Bill framework under Article 199 is exclusively the domain of the Speaker of the Assembly.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 199 vests the Money Bill certification exclusively in the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly. The Chairman of the Council has no power in the Money Bill process — the Council can only make recommendations on a Money Bill, which the Assembly may accept or reject.

statement_analysis.statement: The Governor of a state can summon a joint sitting of the Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council when there is an irresolvable deadlock between the two Houses on a non-Money Bill.
statement_analysis.reason: There is no constitutional provision empowering the Governor to summon a joint sitting of the two Houses of a state legislature. No such mechanism exists — it is a plausible fabrication with no constitutional basis.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only two' tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as correct but mistakenly accept Statement 4 as valid, believing the Governor has residuary powers to summon joint sittings.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: No joint sitting provision exists for state bicameral legislatures — contrast with Article 108 at Centre is accurate. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The claim that Assembly re-passage in the next session automatically overrides the Council is not a constitutional provision for states — this mechanism does not exist. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 199 money bill certification is exclusively the Speaker's — Chairman of Council has no role. Statement 3 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: No constitutional provision allows the Governor to convene a joint sitting — this is fabricated. Statement 4 is incorrect.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct — the answer is (a) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is the most dangerous trap — it deploys a plausible institutional logic (Governor as constitutional head convening joint sittings like the President under Article 108) that students may accept without checking. The answer is that no such provision exists for state legislatures. Statement 2 similarly fabricates a re-passage override mechanism that applies (in modified form) only at the Centre through the joint sitting route — which itself does not exist for states.
solution.final_explanation:
Bicameral state legislatures lack the deadlock-resolution mechanisms available at the Centre, creating a significantly different constitutional dynamic.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Unlike Article 108 at the Centre, there is no constitutional provision for a joint sitting of the State Assembly and Council. Deadlocks between the two Houses in state legislatures cannot be resolved by a joint sitting.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No provision in the Constitution allows the Assembly to override the Council by re-passing a Bill in the next session. The Council's delaying power is its only check on non-Money Bills — there is no override mechanism.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 199 vests Money Bill certification exclusively in the Speaker of the Assembly. The Chairman of the Council has no certification authority — the Council can only make recommendations.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: There is no constitutional provision empowering the Governor to convene a joint sitting of the two Houses of a state legislature. This power does not exist, despite the surface plausibility of the claim.

Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — the answer is (a) Only two.

Value Addition:
• The six bicameral states are UP, Maharashtra, Bihar, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.
• The Council can delay a non-Money Bill by at most one session — this is its maximum delaying power.
• Article 169 allows Parliament to create or abolish a state Legislative Council on the basis of a resolution by the concerned Assembly.

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker votes first instance during removal proceedings unique right
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? A states that during the consideration of a resolution for the Speaker's removal, the Speaker has the right to vote in the first instance — unlike normal proceedings where the Speaker votes only on a tie. This is correct — it is an explicit constitutional provision.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? R states that the Speaker's normal casting vote is intended to preserve the status quo by not changing an existing position. This is an overgeneralisation — the casting vote's purpose is to resolve a tie, not specifically to 'preserve the status quo.' As stated, R is an inaccurate characterisation of why the casting vote exists.
Step 3 — A is correct; R as stated is an inaccurate characterisation and therefore incorrect.
A is correct, R is incorrect — the answer is (c).
solution.final_explanation:
The Speaker's voting rights are context-specific under the Constitution. Two different voting contexts must be distinguished.

Assertion (A) — Correct: During the consideration of a removal resolution under Article 179(c), the Speaker has the right to vote in the first instance — this is the unique exception to the general rule. In all other proceedings, the Speaker does not vote unless there is a tie.

Reason (R) — Incorrect: The characterisation that the casting vote is 'intended to preserve the status quo by not changing an existing position' is a generalisation that overstates the purpose. The casting vote is a procedural mechanism to resolve a tie — its effect (maintaining or changing the status quo) depends on how the Speaker exercises it. The reason as stated is an inaccurate explanation of the casting vote's constitutional purpose.

Since A is correct and R is incorrect, the answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• The casting vote (voting only in case of a tie) is the general rule for the Speaker in ordinary proceedings.
• The first-instance vote during removal proceedings is the specific exception — designed to give the Speaker a full voice in proceedings directly affecting their own tenure.
• The Deputy Speaker has identical voting rights — casting vote normally, first-instance vote during their own removal proceedings.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 194 state legislature privileges freedom of speech immunity
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because Article 19 (freedom of speech as a fundamental right) is better known to students than Article 194, and they may assume the legislature's freedom of speech derives from or is codified under Article 19.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a) Article 19: Article 19 guarantees freedom of speech as a fundamental right to all citizens. Legislative privileges are a separate constitutional framework — Article 19's protections are distinct from parliamentary privilege.
Eliminate (c) Article 212: Article 212 bars courts from inquiring into legislative proceedings — it is about judicial review, not the primary source of members' individual and collective privileges.
Eliminate (d) Article 226: Article 226 relates to High Court writs — entirely unrelated to legislative privileges.
Confirm (b) Article 194: Article 194 is the provision that expressly grants freedom of speech and immunity from court proceedings to members of state legislatures — the correct answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Article 19 trap is the classic error here. Students who remember that freedom of speech is a fundamental right naturally associate it with Article 19. However, legislative privilege (including freedom of speech within the legislature) is a separate and specifically protected category under Article 194 — which provides that no member can be made liable to any court for anything said or voted in the legislature. Article 19 applies to citizens in general; Article 194 applies specifically to legislative privilege.
solution.final_explanation:
The privileges of members of state legislatures are grounded in a specific constitutional provision that is distinct from the general fundamental rights framework.

• Option (a) Article 19 — Incorrect: Article 19 guarantees freedom of speech as a fundamental right for all citizens. Legislative privilege is a separate and higher-order protection specifically for what members say and do within the legislature — it is not derived from Article 19.
• Option (b) Article 194 — Correct: Article 194 expressly provides for collective and individual privileges of state legislature members, including freedom of speech within the legislature and immunity from court proceedings for anything said or voted in the legislature.
• Option (c) Article 212 — Incorrect: Article 212 prevents courts from inquiring into the validity of legislative proceedings — it is a procedural bar on judicial review, not the primary source of members' privileges.
• Option (d) Article 226 — Incorrect: Article 226 relates to the High Court's power to issue writs — entirely unrelated to legislative privileges.

Value Addition:
• Article 194 for state legislatures corresponds to Article 105 for Parliament.
• The privileges under Article 194 include: freedom of speech in the legislature, immunity from court proceedings for votes and speeches, right to regulate internal proceedings, and right to publish debates.
• Courts can intervene if there is an allegation of unconstitutional action — Raja Ram Pal case (2007).

concepts_used: Kihoto Hollohan Case (1992) and Its Implications for Speaker's Powers
Speaker and the Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule)

solution.concept_anchor: Kihoto Hollohan paragraph 7 struck down Speaker as tribunal

statement_analysis.statement: In the Kihoto Hollohan case (1992), the Supreme Court upheld the Tenth Schedule in its entirety without striking down any of its provisions.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court upheld the Tenth Schedule as constitutionally valid but struck down paragraph 7, which had barred judicial review of the Speaker's decisions under the Tenth Schedule. The Schedule was not upheld in its entirety.

statement_analysis.statement: The Kihoto Hollohan case established that the Speaker, when deciding disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule, acts as a tribunal whose decisions have the force of law and are subject to judicial review only after a final order.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court held that the Speaker acts as a 'tribunal' under the Tenth Schedule — the decision is quasi-judicial in nature and has the force of law. However, courts can intervene only after a final order, not during proceedings.

statement_analysis.statement: Following the Kihoto Hollohan judgment, the Speaker's decisions under the Tenth Schedule became completely immune from judicial review, as the Court reasoned that legislative proceedings are internal matters.
statement_analysis.reason: The judgment had the opposite effect — by striking down paragraph 7 (which barred judicial review), the Court made the Speaker's final orders subject to judicial review. The judgment reduced, not increased, the immunity from judicial scrutiny.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) tempts students who confuse the judgment's direction — many recall that Kihoto Hollohan related to judicial review but cannot remember whether it expanded or contracted it.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Kihoto Hollohan struck down paragraph 7 — the Schedule was not upheld in its entirety. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: The Speaker-as-tribunal principle with post-final-order judicial review is exactly what Kihoto Hollohan established. Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: The judgment removed immunity (by striking paragraph 7) rather than creating it — Statement 3 reverses the judgment's actual effect. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statement 2 is correct — the answer is (b) 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 deploys reversed-causation — it states the exact opposite of what the judgment held. Students who partially recall 'Kihoto Hollohan = judicial review issue' but cannot remember the judgment's direction will be drawn to selecting Statement 3 as correct, thinking the Court reinforced immunity. Statement 1 is a scope-extension trap — it claims the entire Schedule was upheld, which is true for most of it but false for paragraph 7.
solution.final_explanation:
Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) is the foundational Supreme Court judgment on the Tenth Schedule's validity and the Speaker's role under it.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Court did NOT uphold the Tenth Schedule in its entirety. It upheld the Schedule's validity but specifically struck down paragraph 7, which had barred courts from questioning the Speaker's decisions under the Tenth Schedule.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The judgment established that when deciding disqualification petitions, the Speaker acts as a 'tribunal' — a quasi-judicial authority. The decision has the force of law. Courts can review it, but only after a final order, not at an interim stage.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: This statement reverses the judgment's actual effect. By striking down paragraph 7, the Court opened the Speaker's decisions to judicial review — the judgment reduced immunity from judicial scrutiny, not increased it.

Only Statement 2 is correct — the answer is (b) 2 only.

Value Addition:
• The Kihoto Hollohan judgment was decided by a 3:2 majority — it was not unanimous.
• The Subhash Desai case (2023) further evolved the position by directing Speakers to decide disqualification petitions within a reasonable time.
• Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule is now void — judicial review of final Speaker orders is available.
